title: Anglo-Saxon England
capsule: Anglo-Saxon England denotes the period of Germanic settlement and kingdom-formation in Britain after the withdrawal of Roman administration in the early fifth century, when Angles, Saxons, and Jutes established competing realms including Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Kent, and Wessex. From the late eighth century Viking raids and the arrival of the Great Heathen Army (865) reshaped the political map, until Alfred the Great of Wessex (r. 871-899) checked the Danes, agreed the Danelaw boundary with Guthrum, and built a network of fortified burhs. Alfred's son Edward the Elder and grandson Æthelstan pressed the reconquest northward; after taking Viking York in 927 Æthelstan was acknowledged as the first king of all the English, a position consolidated by the close of his reign in the 930s.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The general outline of Anglo-Saxon political geography is well-attested through chronicles (the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Bede's Ecclesiastical History) and charter evidence, though exact boundaries between kingdoms shifted frequently and early settlement extent is approximate.
